paras: The York Dispatch lynching warning was a printed threat made in the summer of 1905 by the York Dispatch of York, Pennsylvania, against an unnamed Black man accused of striking a white woman who had stopped a dog fight. No attack on the man is reported, and the episode is known only from a brief item in the Montgomery Advertiser that quoted the Dispatch's warning and its closing word, "Lynching?"

According to the item, a white woman in York "interfered and stopped a dog-fight," which angered a Black man described as "an interested negro." He was accused of striking her with his fist. The York Dispatch then told "the colored gentleman" that he would "see fighting that won't interest him at all if his name leaks out," and added the single word "Lynching?" The item gives neither the man's name nor the date of the incident.
The coverage does not show whether the man was identified, arrested or harmed.

The Montgomery Advertiser printed the item on its fourth page on 26 August 1905 as a short aside on a Northern paper's threat, without comment for or against it. Its wording, calling the man first "an interested negro" and then "the colored gentleman," kept the Dispatch's hint of lynching as the punch line. The York Dispatch's original was not located, and no Black-press coverage of the incident was found.
